I offer her to go but she can't even fit on a bike anymore! All she does is sit around and watch tv, moaning about how the couch creaks when she sits on it and that she's "starving" and "NEEEEEEDS" ice cream or a sundae or slush from Sonic. I've lost my sister to HAES...

All I can offer is to keep trying. It's summer now, so maybe try to get her to go swimming. From a medical POV, it's lower impact, so it'll help with exercising without the usual fat complaints about joint pain, etc. Get her using my fitness pal. Have a serious conversation with her about how you're worried about her, and offer to tackle it together. Depending on how close you are, try to do active things together. I'd bribe my little sister with video games for cutting things out of her diet.

Depending on how worried you are, talk to your parents and see if you can get them to buy healthy foods and make healthy meals. When my mom was diagnosed with diabetes, she got rid of all of her temptations, which resulted in my younger sister also slimming down.

There are a lot of things you can do. If you're the older sibling, chances are she looks up to you. Start with swimming and getting your parents onboard. Use peer-reviewed studies if you need to, but you'll be fighting a losing battle if you have enablers surrounding her.

Spent more than six months in the Air Force Honor Guard a few years ago.

For those of you that don't know what that is, most people recognize the servicemen/women that fold the flag and play TAPS during a funeral... although we did a large number of things.
I was in the US Air Force Honor Guard. AMA
What was the most insane/embarrassing/scary/funniest/depressing thing to occur while performing your duties?

The most depressing thing was delivering a shadow box to a father after the funeral.

It's a long story that I wrote on "the other site" a couple of times, but here's an abridged version:

This guy's 17 yo daughter went into the AF and got sick in Basic. She got so sick so fast that she passed away before they could even diagnose her. When we were tasked to do the funeral, we didn't have anything for her. We would usually make a shadow box, for the folded flag, which was lined with the service member's name plate, the ribbons they were awarded, US insignia, and other things... but she hadn't been in long enough to even have a name plate made for her, none-the-less ribbons awarded.

So, at the funeral, we presented two flags (one for each parent, since they were divorced) and two sets of spent brass. Some people think this is the most difficult part, but we practiced a speech ad nauseam so that it was emotionless and mechanical. The motions and the speech and the final salute was mechanical, so we were able to "remove" ourselves from the situation... so it wasn't as difficult as most people think it is. Now, don't get me wrong, it's still really difficult, but we did what we could to curb the emotion because the ceremony wasn't about us, it was about the deceased.

We later told them that we'd have the shadow boxes at a later time, when we were able to assemble everything appropriately. They agreed and thanked us for our service.

When we finished assembling the boxes, we tried calling the parents to schedule a meeting, but the mother wouldn't answer her phone. The father said that even though he didn't talk to her anymore, he'd make an exception and deliver the box to her for us as a "thank you" for our service.

So me and another HG member got a GOV and drove to his "house." I use quotes because we drove by several times due to the fact that it was a run-down camping trailer in the middle of a trash-ridden field. The man standing in the yard barely resembled the neatly-dressed gentleman in a suit and tie we had met over a week before.

I instantly saw his entire life before my eyes: He had lost his wife, his home, and most of all his only daughter. In his most proud moment, when his daughter left to serve her country, he didn't know it would be the last time he'd see her.

And we pulled into his "driveway" and I carried the two boxes to him... I handed them to him and he looked me in the eye...

This was when I realized I didn't have anything to say to him. I didn't have a prepared speech, and I panicked. I looked back into his eyes and said, "I'm sorry."

He immediately dropped the boxes and hugged me and cried into my neck/shoulder heavier than anyone has ever cried before. My training told me that I should keep my military bearing and stand there, emotionless. So I did the only thing I could do: I hugged him back. I could feel his weight as he just broke down from the weight of the world.

When he was done, he picked up the boxes, looked and me, and thanked me. I watched him walk into his "house" and I went back to my car...
